docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Map Viewer provides an interactive map display for geotagged images by opening Leaflet.js maps in your default web browser.

docs.title: Map Display
docs.text:
• Opens interactive maps in your default web browser
  • Full Leaflet.js functionality and performance
  • Reliable loading of all map components
  • Handles datasets of any size

Note: Maps always open in your default web browser for optimal performance and full Leaflet.js functionality.

Interactive map view opened in web browser with geotagged images displayed as markers

docs.title: Interactive Maps
docs.text:
• Interactive Leaflet.js maps with full functionality (zoom, pan, markers, popups)
  • OpenStreetMap tiles for base layer
  • Color-coded markers for different image types

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• Leaflet.js: JavaScript mapping library (loaded via CDN)
  • OpenStreetMap: Map tile provider
  • webbrowser: Python standard library module for opening URLs

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Maps are displayed in your default web browser for the best user experience.

docs.title: Technical Implementation
docs.text:
• File: src/crackz/gui/components/map_viewer.py
  • Generates Leaflet.js HTML map with geotagged image markers
  • Saves HTML to a temporary file
  • Opens the map in your default web browser using webbrowser.open()
  • Browser provides full JavaScript functionality for interactive maps

docs.title: From GUI
docs.text:
1. Open a project in the Crackz GUI
  2. Click the 🗺️ Map button in the toolbar (or navigate to View > Map View)
  3. Select the data split (raw, train, val, test)
  4. Click "Open in Browser" to view the interactive map
  5. Map opens instantly in your default web browser

docs.title: From Code
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from crackz.gui.components.map_viewer import MapViewerWindow
from crackz.project.project import load_project

# Load a project
project = load_project(Path("path/to/project"))

# Note: MapViewerWindow requires a parent GUI app instance and is typically
# used within the Crackz GUI application. For command-line access to GPS data, use:
from crackz.project.geoposition import get_project_geopositions

# Get GPS data for all images in the project
gps_data = get_project_geopositions(project)
for image_path, geo_pos in gps_data.items():
    print(f"{image_path}: {geo_pos.latitude}, {geo_pos.longitude}")

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
• Blue markers: Images without detections
  • Red markers: Images with crack detections

docs.title: Legend

docs.title: Controls

  • Popups: Click markers to see image names

1. Check Default Browser: Ensure you have a web browser set as default
  2. Check Logs: Look in logs/crackz.log for error messages

docs.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol) Integration
docs.text: Crackz includes built-in support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which enables AI assistants to interact with development tools and services in a standardized way using code execution for maximum efficiency.

docs.title: Quick Facts
docs.text:
• MCP Servers Configured: 4 (filesystem, github, python, uv)
  • Who Uses MCP: Developers only (Claude Desktop, Cline, other MCP-compatible tools)
  • Who Doesn't Use MCP: End users (GUI chat), GitHub Copilot (uses IDE context instead)
  • Purpose: Enable AI development assistants to efficiently interact with files, GitHub, Python, and package management

Note: This documentation is for developers setting up MCP tools. End users of the Crackz GUI do not need MCP configuration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
MCP provides a unified interface for AI assistants to interact with development tools. Crackz is configured with 4 MCP servers:

  1. filesystem - File operations with progressive disclosure
  2. github - GitHub API operations (issues, PRs, releases, workflows)
  3. python - Code execution environment for composing MCP operations
  4. uv - Package manager operations

The configuration follows Anthropic's best practices for code execution with MCP, using code to compose MCP operations efficiently and minimize token consumption.

docs.title: Who Uses MCP?
docs.text:
Development Agents (✅ Uses MCP): - Claude Desktop - Cline (VS Code extension) - Other MCP-compatible AI development tools

GitHub Copilot (❌ No MCP): - Uses IDE context and workspace files directly - Configured via .github/copilot-instructions.md - No MCP servers needed

End-User GUI Chat (❌ No MCP): - Built into Crackz GUI for harbor inspectors - Intentionally kept simple without developer tools - No filesystem, GitHub, or code execution access

docs.title: AI Assistant Comparison
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
│ Development Agents          │ GitHub Copilot       │ End-User GUI        │
├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ ✅ 4 MCP Servers            │ ❌ No MCP            │ ❌ No MCP           │
│   • filesystem              │                      │                     │
│   • github                  │ IDE context          │ Simple API          │
│   • python                  │ Workspace files      │ Project info only   │
│   • uv                      │                      │                     │
├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ Tools: Claude Desktop,      │ Tools: VS Code,      │ Tools: Crackz GUI   │
│        Cline                │        IDE           │        Chat Panel   │
└─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

Key Takeaway: Only 1 of the 3 AI assistant contexts uses MCP servers. MCP is exclusively for developers using tools like Claude Desktop or Cline, not for GitHub Copilot or end-user chat.

docs.title: Code Execution with MCP
docs.text:
Instead of making direct tool calls that pass all data through the model's context window, AI assistants write Python code to:

  • Filter data before returning results: Process large datasets in code, return only relevant information
  • Compose operations efficiently: Loop over operations without alternating tool calls through the model
  • Load tools on-demand: Use progressive disclosure to read tool definitions only when needed
  • Maintain state: Keep intermediate results in the execution environment, not in context

Example - Traditional approach (inefficient): 

TOOL CALL: filesystem.readDirectory("src/")
→ returns 50 files in context

TOOL CALL: filesystem.readFile("src/file1.py")
→ returns full file in context

TOOL CALL: filesystem.readFile("src/file2.py")
→ returns full file in context

Example - Code execution approach (efficient): 

# Discover and filter in code
files = await filesystem.readDirectory("src/")
python_files = [f for f in files if f.endswith(".py")]

# Load only what's needed
for filename in python_files[:5]:  # Top 5 only
    content = await filesystem.readFile(f"src/{filename}")
    # Process in code, log summary only
    print(f"{filename}: {len(content)} lines")

docs.title: Progressive Disclosure
docs.text:
Load tool definitions on-demand rather than upfront:

  1. List directories to discover available modules
  2. Read specific files only when needed
  3. Search for relevant tools before loading full definitions
  4. Keep context lean by loading incrementally

docs.title: AI Assistant Development Standards
docs.text: AI assistants working with Crackz MUST follow these conventions:

docs.title: 1. Branch Naming Convention
docs.text:
Format: <type>/<scope>-<short-slug> (lowercase, hyphenated)

Examples: 

feat/gui-live-preview        # New GUI feature
fix/pdf-rendering-crash      # Bug fix in PDF generation
perf/dataloader-cache        # Performance improvement
docs/api-reference-update    # Documentation update
refactor/config-cleanup      # Code refactoring

docs.title: 2. Commit Message Format
docs.text:
Format: <type>(<scope>): <description> (lowercase type with colon)

Examples: 

feat(gui): add real-time detection preview
fix(cli): correct path handling in Windows
perf(dataloader): implement batch caching
docs(api): update training configuration reference

docs.title: 3. Pull Request Title Format (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
The PR title MUST follow conventional commit format to trigger releases!

Format: <type>(<scope>): <description>

✅ CORRECT (triggers release): 

feat(gui): add export panel for detection results
fix(pdf): handle missing hero image gracefully
perf(training): optimize data loading pipeline

❌ INCORRECT (no release triggered): 

Fix GUI bugs and add new feature
Update documentation
Add export functionality

Release Triggers: - feat: or feat(<scope>): → MINOR version bump (1.2.0 → 1.3.0) - fix: or fix(<scope>): → PATCH version bump (1.2.0 → 1.2.1) - perf: or perf(<scope>): → PATCH version bump (1.2.0 → 1.2.1)

No Release (maintenance): - docs: - Documentation changes only - refactor: - Code restructuring without behavior changes - test: - Test-only changes - chore: - Maintenance, dependencies, tooling - ci: - CI/CD pipeline changes - build: - Build system or Docker changes

docs.title: 4. Code Quality Standards
docs.text:
CLI Commands: - Use typer.secho() with colors for user messages - Use logger from crackz.log for operational details - Import centralized options from crackz.cli.options - Never use print() statements

Testing: - Add/update unit tests for all behavior changes - Maintain minimum 75% test coverage - Run tests before committing: uv run task tests

Type Safety: - Add type hints to all public interfaces - Run mypy: uv run task mypy

See Contributing Guide for complete details.

docs.title: Initialize MCP Configuration
docs.text:
Create a default MCP configuration file:

crackz mcp init

This creates .mcp/config.json with sensible defaults for the Crackz project.

docs.title: View Configuration
docs.text:
Display the current MCP configuration:

crackz mcp show

docs.title: Validate Configuration
docs.text:
Check that the configuration is valid:

crackz mcp validate

docs.title: Configuration Structure
docs.text: The MCP configuration is a JSON file (.mcp/config.json) with servers, metadata, and patterns sections:

docs.title: MCP Servers (4 Total)
docs.text:
Crackz is configured with 4 MCP servers available to AI development assistants:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."],
      "description": "Filesystem operations with progressive disclosure"
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": {
        "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      },
      "description": "GitHub operations (issues, PRs, releases)"
    },
    "python": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-python"],
      "description": "Python code execution environment"
    },
    "uv": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-uv"],
      "description": "UV package manager operations"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Provides context about the project:

{
  "metadata": {
    "project": "Crackz",
    "language": "python",
    "version": "3.13",
    "package_manager": "uv",
    "framework": "pytorch-lightning",
    "cli": "typer",
    "gui": "customtkinter",
    "testing": "pytest",
    "ci": "github-actions",
    "release": "semantic-release",
    "code_execution": true,
    "progressive_disclosure": true
  }
}

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
Defines recommended usage patterns:

{
  "patterns": {
    "code_execution": {
      "enabled": true,
      "description": "Use code execution to interact with MCP servers efficiently",
      "examples": [
        "Filter large datasets in code before returning results",
        "Loop over operations without alternating tool calls",
        "Compose multiple MCP operations in a single execution"
      ]
    },
    "progressive_disclosure": {
      "enabled": true,
      "description": "Load tool definitions on-demand",
      "workflow": [
        "List directories to discover modules",
        "Read specific files as needed",
        "Load documentation when relevant"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: crackz mcp init
docs.text:
Initialize a new MCP configuration file.

Options: - --output / -o: Output path for config file (default: .mcp/config.json) - --force / -f: Overwrite existing config file

Examples:

# Create with defaults
crackz mcp init

# Create in custom location
crackz mcp init --output custom/mcp.json

# Overwrite existing config
crackz mcp init --force

docs.title: crackz mcp show
docs.text:
Display the current MCP configuration with syntax highlighting.

Options: - --config / -c: Path to config file (default: .mcp/config.json)

Examples:

# Show default config
crackz mcp show

# Show custom config
crackz mcp show --config custom/mcp.json

docs.title: crackz mcp validate
docs.text:
Validate that the MCP configuration is well-formed and follows the expected schema.

Options: - --config / -c: Path to config file (default: .mcp/config.json)

Examples:

# Validate default config
crackz mcp validate

# Validate custom config
crackz mcp validate --config custom/mcp.json

docs.title: Adding Custom Servers
docs.text:
Add your own MCP-compatible servers to .mcp/config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": { ... },
    "custom-api": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["./custom-mcp-server.js"],
      "description": "Custom MCP server for specialized operations"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Extending Metadata
docs.text:
Add custom project metadata:

{
  "metadata": {
    "project": "Crackz",
    "language": "python",
    "team": "ML Ops",
    "repository": "https://github.com/Anaxiatech-AB/crackz",
    "custom_field": "your_value"
  }
}

docs.title: Integration with AI Assistants
docs.text:
AI assistants that support MCP can use this configuration to:

  1. Execute Python code: Write code to compose MCP operations efficiently
  2. Use progressive disclosure: Load tool definitions on-demand to minimize tokens
  3. Filter data in code: Process large results before passing to context
  4. Understand project context: Access metadata about language, frameworks, and tools
  5. Maintain state: Keep intermediate results in execution environment

docs.title: Code Execution Best Practices
docs.text:
DO: - Write Python code to filter and transform data before returning results - Use loops and conditionals in code rather than chaining tool calls - Load only the files and tools you need for the current task - Keep intermediate data in the execution environment

DON'T: - Pass large datasets through the model context unnecessarily - Load all tool definitions upfront - Make sequential tool calls when a loop would be more efficient - Return raw data when a summary would suffice

docs.title: Example Workflows
docs.text:
Efficient file discovery: 

# List Python files in src/
files = await filesystem.readDirectory("src/crackz")
py_files = [f for f in files if f.endswith(".py")]

# Read only the first 3 for initial analysis
for filename in py_files[:3]:
    content = await filesystem.readFile(f"src/crackz/{filename}")
    lines = len(content.split('\n'))
    print(f"{filename}: {lines} lines")

Efficient GitHub operations: 

# Get recent PRs and filter in code
prs = await github.listPullRequests(repo="Anaxiatech-AB/crackz", state="open")
priority_prs = [pr for pr in prs if "feat:" in pr.title or "fix:" in pr.title]

print(f"Found {len(priority_prs)} priority PRs out of {len(prs)} total")
for pr in priority_prs[:5]:  # Show top 5 only
    print(f"#{pr.number}: {pr.title}")

Efficient package operations: 

# Install multiple packages in one operation
packages = ["pytest", "ruff", "mypy"]
for pkg in packages:
    await uv.install(package=pkg)
    print(f"✓ Installed {pkg}")

docs.title: Default Configuration
docs.text:
The default MCP configuration for Crackz includes:

  • Filesystem: Progressive discovery and file operations
  • Python: Code execution environment for composing operations
  • UV: Package management with uv tooling
  • GitHub: Version control operations (issues, PRs, releases)

This configuration follows Anthropic's best practices for code execution with MCP to minimize token usage and maximize agent efficiency.

docs.title: Logging Practices
docs.text: Crackz uses Loguru for logging with a hybrid approach: central logs + per-project logs.

docs.title: When to Use Logging
docs.text:
Use logger for: - Operational/detailed information (progress updates, technical details) - Internal state changes and debugging information - Warnings about internal conditions - Error details for troubleshooting - Any information useful for debugging or auditing

DO NOT use print() statements - Always use the logger instead.

docs.title: Logging Locations
docs.text:
1. Central Log: System-wide log for all Crackz operations
  2. Location priority: CRACKZ_LOG_DIR env var > --log-dir CLI flag > system temp directory
  3. Contains all logging output from all projects and operations

  4. Useful for debugging across multiple projects

  5. Project Log: Per-project log at <project>/logs/

  6. Always stored relative to the project directory
  7. Contains only logs specific to that project's operations
  8. Automatically created when project operations run

docs.title: Logging Examples
docs.text: ```python from crackz.log import logger

docs.title: Info level - operational progress
docs.text: logger.info("Starting image import for {} files", len(files))

docs.title: Warning level - non-critical issues
docs.text: logger.warning("Mask not found for image {}, skipping", image_name)

docs.title: Error level - failures with details
docs.text: logger.error("Failed to load checkpoint: {}", error, exc_info=True)

docs.title: Debug level - detailed troubleshooting info
docs.text: logger.debug("Model config: encoder={}, weights={}", encoder, weights)

docs.text:

  • CLI Reference
  • Contributing Guide
  • API Reference

docs.title: Project Schema Migration
docs.text: Crackz versions project YAML files with a simple integer schema_version field. When new optional fields are added (e.g. ai.training.tensorboard) the schema version increases and a lightweight in-place migration is available.

docs.title: When Migration Is Needed
docs.text:
You may need migration if: - Your project YAML has no schema_version field (legacy v0) - The value is lower than the current CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION exposed by crackz.project.migration

Migration adds any missing defaulted fields and stamps the new schema_version. It never removes user data.

docs.title: Schema Version History
docs.text: Version Changes Notes 0 (legacy) No schema_version field, no ai.training.tensorboard Original projects created before versioning 1 Added schema_version: 1 and ai.training.tensorboard: false First versioned schema 2 Added data section with mask_threshold: 1 Binary mask conversion support 3 New artifacts structure + project.crackz_version tracking Current version - Improved organization

docs.title: Version 3 Changes (Current)
docs.text:
Schema version 3 introduces improved artifacts organization and version tracking:

schema_version: 3
project:
  name: my_project
  description: My crack detection project
  created: '2025-01-15T10:30:00Z'
  crackz_version: '0.50.0'  # NEW: Tracks Crackz app version

What gets added: - project.crackz_version: Tracks which Crackz version created/last modified the project - New artifacts directory structure (backward compatible): - checkpoints/ to models/ (clearer purpose for model weights) - runtime/ for temporary artifacts (TensorBoard, Lightning logs) - detections/visualizations/ for PNG detection outputs

Backward compatibility: - Old projects continue working - checkpoints_path checks legacy checkpoints/ directory first - New writes automatically use improved structure (models/, runtime/, etc.) - File migration available - optionally migrate existing files to new structure - Migration only updates schema version and adds crackz_version field by default

docs.title: Version 2 Changes
docs.text:
Schema version 2 introduced the data configuration section:

data:
  mask_threshold: 1
schema_version: 2

Added data.mask_threshold for binary mask conversion during image import.

docs.title: CLI Auto / Assisted Migration
docs.text:
Most CLI commands that load a project (e.g. detect train, detect run, image imports, exporting configs, pruning checkpoints) now check the schema version and will:

  1. Interactive terminal:
  2. Prompt: Project schema v0 < v1. Migrate now? [y/N]:
  3. On Yes: Runs in-place migration with a .bak backup.
  4. Non-interactive (CI, pipelines):
  5. If CRACKZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=1 is set, migration runs automatically.
  6. Otherwise a guidance message is printed and the old schema is used.

docs.title: Manual Migration Command
docs.text:
Use the explicit command to inspect or apply migrations:

crackz migrate --project <path-to-project-dir>
# or
crackz migrate --cfg <path-to-project-yaml>

Common flags: - --dry-run : Show what would change without writing. - --no-backup : Skip writing <file>.bak before overwrite. - --migrate-files : NEW Also migrate artifacts directory structure (checkpoints to models, etc.)

docs.title: Schema-Only Migration (Default)
docs.text:
Basic migration only updates the YAML schema and adds missing fields:

# Using project directory
crackz migrate --project my_project --dry-run
crackz migrate --project my_project

# Using direct YAML file path
crackz migrate --cfg my_project/my_project_project.yaml

docs.title: File Migration (Optional)
docs.text:
NEW in v3: Optionally migrate the actual artifacts directory structure:

# Preview what files would be moved
crackz migrate --project my_project --migrate-files --dry-run

# Migrate both schema AND files
crackz migrate --project my_project --migrate-files

File migration moves: - checkpoints/ to models/ - training/tensorboard/ to runtime/tensorboard/ - training/lightning_logs/ to runtime/lightning_logs/ - detections/*.png to detections/visualizations/

Safety features: - Always creates backup of entire artifacts directory before moving files - Interactive confirmation before proceeding - Automatic rollback if migration fails - Detailed progress reporting

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
By default, a timestamped backup is created before modifying the original project file. Backup files use the format: {filename}.v{version}.{timestamp}.bak

Example: 

myproject_project.v2.20250115_143022.bak

This format includes: - Version number (v2) - Shows which schema version this backup came from - Timestamp (20250115_143022) - UTC timestamp ensures unique backups per migration - Multiple migrations create multiple backups (never overwrites previous backups)

To revert a migration: 1. Locate the timestamped backup file (e.g., myproject_project.v2.20250115_143022.bak) 2. Remove or rename the current YAML file 3. Rename the backup file to remove the .v2.20250115_143022.bak suffix

Benefits: - Never lose migration history (each migration creates a unique backup) - Easy to identify which version a backup came from - Can rollback to any previous migration step if needed

docs.title: Environment Variable Summary
docs.text: Variable Effect CRACKZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=1 Auto-migrate without prompt in non-interactive sessions

docs.title: Programmatic Migration
docs.text:
You can call the library function directly:

from pathlib import Path
from crackz.project.migration import migrate_project_file

result = migrate_project_file(Path("my_project"))  # or path/to_yaml
print(result)
# Example result:
# {
#   'status': 'migrated',
#   'from_version': 2,
#   'to_version': 3,
#   'steps': ['2->3: updated to artifacts structure v3 + added crackz_version tracking'],
#   'path': 'my_project/my_project_project.yaml',
#   'backup_path': 'my_project/my_project_project.v2.20250115_143022.bak',
#   'dry_run': False
# }

The result dict contains: - status: "migrated", "noop", or "up-to-date" - from_version: Original schema version - to_version: Final schema version - steps: List of migration step descriptions - path: Path to migrated file - backup_path: Path to backup file (if created) - dry_run: Whether this was a dry run

docs.title: Automated Migration Detection
docs.text:
When opening a project in the GUI, automatic detection occurs for:

  1. Schema Migration: Always prompted and performed when project schema is outdated
  2. File Migration: Detects when artifacts directory structure needs updating

docs.title: Schema Migration Dialog
docs.text: When opening a project with an old schema version, the GUI displays a dialog offering migration. A backup is created automatically; declining leaves the project untouched.

docs.title: File Migration Dialog (NEW)
docs.text:
When artifacts directory structure is outdated, the GUI displays an informational dialog explaining: - Benefits of the new structure (better organization, clearer separation) - Safety measures (backup creation, rollback capability) - User options: "Migrate", "Skip", or "Cancel"

The migration process shows progress and handles any errors gracefully with automatic rollback.

docs.title: Safety and Idempotence
docs.text: Running migration on an already up-to-date project is a no-op. Repeated runs after success make no further changes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Resolution Prompt appears every run Write failed, read-only filesystem Ensure write permissions to project directory Field still missing after migration Uncommitted manual edits reverted defaults Re-run migration or add field manually Many .bak files accumulate Multiple migrations over time Safe to delete old backups after verifying current project works Need to rollback migration Migration caused issues Rename timestamped .bak file to remove suffix and replace current YAML

docs.title: Printable / PDF Export
docs.text:
📄 Crackz Full Documentation · Anaxiatech AB

Generate (or after deployment, download) a single PDF containing the full Crackz documentation, enriched with an outline, styled cover (hero image + logo), bookmarks, and footer page numbers.

The PDF is produced at: site/crackz-docs.pdf after you run an export (not committed). On GitHub Pages deployment you can also upload it as an artifact.

docs.text: If the print-site plugin combined page is absent/empty, the exporter synthesizes a combined HTML page by extracting each built page’s <article> content in navigation order, then applies a print-focused stylesheet (gradient headings, subdued body text, dual-column outline) and inlines images.

docs.title: ChromaDB vs Neo4j: Database Technology Comparison for RAG and Knowledge Graphs
docs.text: Document Version: 1.0 Date: November 2025 Related Issues: #311 (Epic), #312-315 (RAG Phase 1), #316 (Evaluation), #317-321 (KG Phase 3) Related Document: PRODUCT_ROADMAP.md (root directory)

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: This document provides a comprehensive comparison of ChromaDB and Neo4j for the Crackz project's RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and Knowledge Graph implementations.

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
ChromaDB and Neo4j are fundamentally different database technologies that solve different problems:

  • ChromaDB: Vector database optimized for semantic similarity search (RAG/retrieval)
  • Neo4j: Graph database optimized for relationship analysis and traversal

docs.title: Recommendations for Crackz
docs.text: Phase Technology Status Rationale Phase 1 (Q1 2025) ChromaDB ✅ Approved Perfect fit for RAG semantic search, low complexity, embedded mode Phase 2 (Q2 2025) Evaluation ⏳ Pending Critical decision point after 3 months RAG production Phase 3 (Q3-Q4 2025) Neo4j ⚠️ Conditional Only if evaluation validates complex query needs and data volume

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text: Aspect ChromaDB Neo4j Purpose Find similar items Find connected items Data Model Vector embeddings Nodes + relationships Query "What's similar to X?" "How is A related to B?" Deployment Embedded/server Server only Cost (Year 1) $45-125K $135-320K Timeline 4-8 weeks 12-20 weeks Crackz Use Case RAG for AI chat Analytical queries

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. ChromaDB: Vector Database Fundamentals
  2. Neo4j: Graph Database Fundamentals
  3. Core Differences
  4. Context for Crackz Project
  5. Detailed Comparison Matrix
  6. Alternatives Analysis
  7. Complementary Usage (Hybrid Architecture)
  8. Implementation Recommendations
  9. Decision Framework
  10. References

docs.title: What is ChromaDB?
docs.text:
ChromaDB is an open-source vector database specifically designed for AI applications. It stores and searches vector embeddings to identify semantically similar information. ChromaDB is optimized for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) workflows where language models need relevant context from large document collections.

Core Concept: Instead of storing text directly, ChromaDB converts documents into high-dimensional vectors (embeddings) that capture semantic meaning. Similar concepts cluster together in vector space, enabling fast similarity search.

docs.title: Developer-First Design
docs.text:
• Simple Python API: 3 lines to get started
  • Zero configuration: Works out-of-the-box for prototyping
  • Flexible embeddings: Supports OpenAI, Sentence Transformers, Cohere, or custom models
  • Multi-modal: Handles text, images, and other data types

docs.title: Performance (2025 Update)
docs.text:
• Rust-core rewrite: 4x performance improvement over previous versions
  • Billion-scale: Handles billions of embeddings in cloud mode
  • Sub-millisecond queries: Fast retrieval for small-medium datasets
  • HNSW indexing: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs for efficient nearest-neighbor search

docs.title: Search Capabilities
docs.text:
• Vector similarity: Cosine distance, L2 distance, or inner product
  • Full-text search: Traditional keyword-based search
  • Metadata filtering: Filter by document properties before similarity search
  • Hybrid search: Combine vector and keyword search

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: ChromaDB offers three deployment modes:

docs.title: 1. Embedded Mode (Development)
docs.text:
import chromadb

# Runs entirely in-process, no separate server
client = chromadb.Client(Settings(
    persist_directory="./chroma_data"
))

Characteristics: - Zero infrastructure overhead - SQLite-based local persistence - Perfect for development and small datasets (<1M vectors) - Runs in the same process as your application

docs.title: 2. Client-Server Mode (Production)
docs.text:
import chromadb

# Connect to separate ChromaDB server
client = chromadb.HttpClient(host="localhost", port=8000)

Characteristics: - Separate server process for scalability - Multiple clients can connect - Better resource isolation - Supports horizontal scaling

docs.title: 3. Managed Cloud Mode (Enterprise)
docs.text:
• Fully managed service with auto-scaling
  • High availability and backup
  • No operational overhead
  • Pay-per-use pricing

docs.title: Storage Technology
docs.text:
Three-Tier Storage: 1. In-Memory Cache: Hot data for sub-millisecond access 2. Local Persistence: SQLite for embedded mode, RocksDB for server mode 3. Distributed Storage: Cloud object storage (S3, GCS) for massive scale

Indexing: - Uses HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs - Optimized for high-dimensional spaces (typical: 384-1536 dimensions) - Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search with tunable accuracy/speed tradeoff

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
import chromadb
from chromadb.config import Settings

# Initialize client
client = chromadb.Client(Settings(
    persist_directory="./data",
    anonymized_telemetry=False
))

# Create or get collection
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="crackz_docs",
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}  # Use cosine similarity
)

# Add documents
collection.add(
    documents=["Training failed due to OOM error", "Model accuracy is 92%"],
    metadatas=[{"type": "log", "project": "harbor1"}, {"type": "metric", "project": "harbor1"}],
    ids=["log_001", "metric_001"]
)

# Query by similarity
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["memory issues during training"],
    n_results=5,
    where={"project": "harbor1"}  # Metadata filtering
)

print(results["documents"])  # Most similar documents
print(results["distances"])  # Similarity scores

docs.title: Advanced Features
docs.text:
# Custom embeddings (bring your own)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

collection.add(
    embeddings=model.encode(["text1", "text2"]).tolist(),
    documents=["text1", "text2"],
    ids=["id1", "id2"]
)

# Hybrid search (vector + keyword)
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["training error"],
    n_results=10,
    where_document={"$contains": "OOM"}  # Full-text filter
)

docs.title: Use Cases & Strengths
docs.text:
Excellent for: - Semantic search: Find documents by meaning, not just keywords - RAG systems: Retrieve relevant context for LLM prompts - Recommendation: Similar content discovery - Question answering: Find relevant passages from knowledge bases - Deduplication: Find near-duplicate documents - Anomaly detection: Find outliers in vector space

Real-World Examples in Crackz Context: - "Find documentation about memory errors" → Retrieves docs mentioning "OOM", "out of memory", "CUDA error", etc. - "Show similar training runs" → Finds runs with similar hyperparameters and performance - "What does the guide say about thresholds?" → Semantic search across all guides

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
Metric Small (<100K vectors) Medium (100K-10M) Large (10M-1B+) Query Latency <1ms 1-10ms 10-100ms Throughput 10,000+ QPS 1,000-5,000 QPS 100-1,000 QPS Memory 1-2GB 4-16GB 32GB+ (or cloud) Storage 100MB-1GB 1-10GB 10GB-1TB+ Deployment Embedded Server Cloud managed

For Crackz (estimated): - Documentation: ~60 files × ~1000 chunks = 60K vectors - Training metrics: ~100 projects × ~10 runs = 1K vectors - Detection results: ~100 projects × ~100 images = 10K vectors - Total: ~71K vectors → Small category (embedded mode works perfectly)

docs.title: Development (Embedded Mode): FREE
docs.text:
• Zero infrastructure cost
  • Runs on your existing hardware
  • Perfect for projects with <1M vectors
  • No external dependencies

docs.title: Production (Self-Hosted)
docs.text: Scale Infrastructure Cost/Month Small (<1M vectors) 2-4GB RAM VPS $20-50 Medium (1-10M) 8GB RAM server $100-200 Large (10M+) Dedicated server + SSD $500-1000

docs.title: Managed Cloud (Varies by Provider)
docs.text:
• Typical pricing: $0.10-0.50 per 1M vectors/month
  • Additional costs for queries and storage
  • Scales automatically with usage

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
What ChromaDB is NOT good for: - ❌ Complex relationship queries ("Which encoder was used by checkpoints that came from models trained on datasets with >500 images?") - ❌ Graph traversal (parent-child relationships, lineage tracking) - ❌ Transactional updates (not ACID-compliant for multi-step operations) - ❌ Analytical aggregations across relationships - ❌ Time-series analysis with entity relationships

Workarounds: - Use metadata filtering for simple relationships - Store pre-aggregated data - Use hybrid approach with separate analytical database

docs.title: What is Neo4j?
docs.text:
Neo4j is a native graph database that stores data as nodes, relationships, and properties. Unlike traditional databases that treat relationships as foreign keys, Neo4j makes relationships first-class citizens with the same status as entities. This enables efficient traversal of complex, interconnected data.

Core Concept: Data is a graph: entities are nodes, connections are relationships. Queries traverse this graph to answer questions like "How is A connected to B?" or "What's the shortest path from X to Y?"

docs.title: Cypher Query Language
docs.text:
Neo4j uses Cypher, a declarative graph query language similar to SQL but optimized for pattern matching.

Example Query: 

// Find best encoder for low-light harbor images
MATCH (tr:TrainingRun)-[:USES_MODEL]->(m:Model),
      (tr)-[:TRAINED_ON]->(ds:Dataset)-[:CONTAINS_IMAGE]->(img:Image),
      (tr)-[:PRODUCED_CHECKPOINT]->(ckpt:Checkpoint)
WHERE img.exif_iso > 800  // Low-light condition
  AND ds.domain = "harbor"
RETURN m.encoder,
       AVG(ckpt.val_iou) as avg_iou,
       COUNT(tr) as num_runs
ORDER BY avg_iou DESC
LIMIT 5

As of 2025: - Cypher 5: Frozen, only bug fixes (backward compatibility) - Cypher 25: Active development, new features monthly

docs.title: Native Graph Storage
docs.text:
• Index-free adjacency: Relationships stored physically with nodes
  • O(1) relationship traversal: No expensive joins
  • Pointer-based navigation: Traverse millions of hops in milliseconds

docs.title: ACID Compliance
docs.text:
• Full transactional support
  • Consistency guarantees
  • Rollback on failure
  • Isolation levels configurable

docs.title: Rich Graph Algorithms
docs.text: Built-in algorithms for: - Pathfinding: Shortest path, all paths, Dijkstra, A - Centrality: PageRank, betweenness, closeness - Community detection: Louvain, label propagation - Similarity: Node similarity, Jaccard, overlap - Link prediction*: Predict future relationships

docs.title: Server-Based Deployment
docs.text:
Unlike ChromaDB's embedded option, Neo4j always runs as a separate server process.

Components: - Neo4j Server: Core database engine - Bolt Protocol: Binary protocol for client-server communication (port 7687) - HTTP API: RESTful API for management (port 7474) - Neo4j Browser: Web-based query interface

Storage: - Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) for durability - Cache-heavy architecture (hot data in RAM) - Separate stores for nodes, relationships, properties, indexes

docs.title: Deployment Options
docs.text:
1. Neo4j Desktop (Development)
  2. Free GUI-based local instance
  3. Includes Neo4j Browser and Bloom visualization

  4. Perfect for development and learning

  5. Self-Hosted Server

  6. Docker: Quick deployment with docker run
  7. Kubernetes: Helm charts available for orchestration

  8. Bare Metal: Native installation on Linux/Windows/Mac

  9. Neo4j Aura (Managed Cloud)

  10. Fully managed, auto-scaling
  11. High availability with automatic failover
  12. Backup and monitoring included

  13. Pricing tiers: Professional ($65-500/mo), Enterprise (custom)

  14. Enterprise Cluster

  15. Multi-datacenter replication
  16. Load balancing
  17. Causal clustering for consistency
  18. Enterprise Edition licensing required

docs.title: Using Official Driver
docs.text:
from neo4j import GraphDatabase

# Connect to Neo4j
driver = GraphDatabase.driver(
    "bolt://localhost:7687",
    auth=("neo4j", "password")
)

# Execute query
def find_best_encoder(tx, min_iso):
    query = """
    MATCH (tr:TrainingRun)-[:USES_MODEL]->(m:Model),
          (tr)-[:PRODUCED_CHECKPOINT]->(ckpt:Checkpoint),
          (tr)-[:TRAINED_ON]->(ds:Dataset)-[:CONTAINS_IMAGE]->(img:Image)
    WHERE img.exif_iso >= $min_iso
    RETURN m.encoder, AVG(ckpt.val_iou) as avg_iou
    ORDER BY avg_iou DESC
    LIMIT 5
    """
    result = tx.run(query, min_iso=min_iso)
    return [{"encoder": record["encoder"], "iou": record["avg_iou"]}
            for record in result]

# Execute in transaction
with driver.session() as session:
    results = session.execute_read(find_best_encoder, min_iso=800)
    print(results)

driver.close()

docs.title: Creating Graph Data
docs.text:
def create_training_run(tx, run_data):
    query = """
    // Create training run
    CREATE (tr:TrainingRun {
        id: $run_id,
        started_at: datetime($started_at),
        epochs: $epochs
    })

    // Connect to model
    MATCH (m:Model {encoder: $encoder})
    CREATE (tr)-[:USES_MODEL]->(m)

    // Create checkpoint
    CREATE (ckpt:Checkpoint {
        name: $ckpt_name,
        val_iou: $val_iou,
        epoch: $best_epoch
    })
    CREATE (tr)-[:PRODUCED_CHECKPOINT]->(ckpt)

    RETURN tr, ckpt
    """
    result = tx.run(query, **run_data)
    return result.single()

with driver.session() as session:
    session.execute_write(create_training_run, {
        "run_id": "run_001",
        "started_at": "2025-01-15T10:00:00",
        "epochs": 50,
        "encoder": "resnet34",
        "ckpt_name": "best.ckpt",
        "val_iou": 0.87,
        "best_epoch": 42
    })

docs.title: Use Cases & Strengths
docs.text:
Excellent for: - Relationship analysis: "How are these entities connected?" - Lineage tracking: Model ancestry, data provenance - Pattern detection: Fraud, anomalies in network behavior - Recommendation: Graph-based collaborative filtering - Impact analysis: "If I change X, what's affected?" - Network analysis: Social networks, infrastructure dependencies - Multi-hop queries: "Friend of friend", "dependency chains"

Real-World Examples in Crackz Context: - "Which encoder works best for harbor images in low light with <500 training samples?" - "Show me the checkpoint lineage for this model" (transfer learning ancestry) - "Track crack severity progression at GPS location X over the last 6 months" - "What hyperparameters were used by the top-performing models on similar datasets?"

docs.title: Query Performance

docs.title: Issue #312: Document Indexing Pipeline
docs.text:
Scope: Index all markdown documentation and configuration schemas

Why ChromaDB is Perfect: 

# Simple integration with existing AIChatService
from chromadb import Client

class DocumentIndexer:
    def __init__(self, persist_directory: Path):
        self.client = Client(Settings(persist_directory=str(persist_directory)))
        self.collection = self.client.get_or_create_collection("crackz_docs")

    def index_documentation(self, docs_dir: Path):
        # Chunk markdown files by headings
        documents = []
        metadatas = []

        for md_file in docs_dir.glob("**/*.md"):
            chunks = self._chunk_by_heading(md_file)
            for chunk in chunks:
                documents.append(chunk.text)
                metadatas.append({
                    "source": str(md_file),
                    "section": chunk.heading,
                    "type": "documentation"
                })

        # Embed and index automatically
        self.collection.add(
            documents=documents,
            metadatas=metadatas,
            ids=[f"doc_{i}" for i in range(len(documents))]
        )

Benefits: - Embedded mode: No separate server setup required - Auto-embedding: ChromaDB generates embeddings automatically - Persistence: Data saved to disk, survives restarts - Simple metadata: Filter by source, section, type

Estimated Data: - 60+ markdown files - ~1000 chunks (avg 200 words each) - ~1000 embeddings (768-dimensional) - Total storage: ~50MB

docs.title: Issue #313: Training and Detection Result Indexing
docs.text:
Scope: Index training metrics and detection results

Why ChromaDB Works: 

def index_training_run(self, project: Project):
    metrics_path = project.paths.artifacts / "training" / "training_metrics.json"

    with open(metrics_path) as f:
        metrics = json.load(f)

    # Create natural language summary for embedding
    summary = f"""
    Training run for project {project.name}:
    - Encoder: {metrics['encoder']}
    - Best validation IoU: {metrics['best_val_iou']:.3f} at epoch {metrics['best_epoch']}
    - Learning rate: {metrics['hyperparameters']['learning_rate']}
    - Batch size: {metrics['hyperparameters']['batch_size']}
    - Dataset: {metrics['train_images']} train, {metrics['val_images']} validation
    - Stopped early: {metrics.get('stopped_early', False)}
    """

    self.collection.add(
        documents=[summary],
        metadatas=[{
            "type": "training_result",
            "project": project.name,
            "encoder": metrics['encoder'],
            "val_iou": metrics['best_val_iou'],
            "timestamp": metrics['timestamp']
        }],
        ids=[f"training_{project.name}_{metrics['timestamp']}"]
    )

Benefits: - Semantic search: "What learning rate worked well?" finds relevant runs - Metadata filtering: Filter by project, encoder, IoU range - Incremental indexing: Add new results as they're generated - No schema changes needed

Estimated Data: - ~100 projects × ~10 training runs = 1,000 training summaries - ~100 projects × ~100 detection results = 10,000 detection records - Total: ~11,000 embeddings (~80MB)

docs.title: Issue #314: RAG Integration into AIChatService
docs.text:
Scope: Integrate retrieval step before Claude API call

Why ChromaDB Fits: 

class AIChatService:
    def __init__(self, ..., enable_rag: bool = True):
        self.enable_rag = enable_rag
        if enable_rag:
            self.retriever = RAGRetriever(rag_index_path)

    async def _call_claude_api(self) -> str:
        # Base system prompt
        system_prompt = self._build_base_system_prompt()

        # Existing project context
        project_context = self._get_context()

        # NEW: RAG retrieval using ChromaDB
        rag_context = ""
        if self.retriever and self.conversation_history:
            last_message = self.conversation_history[-1].content

            # Retrieve relevant docs (ChromaDB query)
            retrieved_docs = await self.retriever.retrieve(
                query=last_message,
                k=5,
                filters={"project": self.app_state.project.name}
            )

            rag_context = self._format_retrieved_docs(retrieved_docs)

        # Combine all context
        full_prompt = f"{system_prompt}\n\n{project_context}\n\n{rag_context}"

        # Call Claude with enhanced context
        response = await client.messages.create(
            model=self.model,
            system=full_prompt,
            messages=self.conversation_history
        )

        return response.content[0].text

Benefits: - <500ms retrieval latency (fast enough for chat) - Seamless integration with existing architecture - Optional: Can be disabled for debugging - Source attribution: Show which docs were retrieved

docs.title: Knowledge Graph Plan (Issues #317-321)
docs.text: Goal: Enable complex analytical queries across training runs, models, and detection results.

docs.title: Issue #317: Knowledge Graph Schema Design
docs.text:
Scope: Design Neo4j graph ontology

Why Neo4j is Recommended:

Complex Domain Model: 

// Rich entity-relationship structure
(Project)-[:HAS_TRAINING_RUN]->(TrainingRun)
(TrainingRun)-[:USES_MODEL]->(Model)
(TrainingRun)-[:TRAINED_ON]->(Dataset)
(TrainingRun)-[:PRODUCED_CHECKPOINT]->(Checkpoint)
(Checkpoint)-[:FINE_TUNED_FROM]->(Checkpoint)  // Lineage!
(Dataset)-[:CONTAINS_IMAGE]->(Image)
(Image)-[:HAS_GPS]->(GPSLocation)
(DetectionRun)-[:PROCESSED_IMAGE]->(Image)
(DetectionRun)-[:USED_CHECKPOINT]->(Checkpoint)
(Crack)-[:DETECTED_IN_IMAGE]->(Image)
(Crack)-[:AT_LOCATION]->(GPSLocation)

This graph model is impossible with ChromaDB because: - No way to represent explicit relationships - No graph traversal capabilities - No path-finding or pattern matching

Example Queries Requiring Graph: 

// 1. Transfer learning recommendation
MATCH path = (ckpt:Checkpoint)-[:FINE_TUNED_FROM*]->(root:Checkpoint)
WHERE ckpt.name = "latest.ckpt"
RETURN path

// 2. Crack progression tracking
MATCH (loc:GPSLocation)<-[:AT_LOCATION]-(img1:Image)<-[:DETECTED_IN_IMAGE]-(crack1:Crack),
      (loc)<-[:AT_LOCATION]-(img2:Image)<-[:DETECTED_IN_IMAGE]-(crack2:Crack)
WHERE crack1.timestamp < crack2.timestamp
  AND crack2.area > crack1.area * 1.2  // 20% growth
RETURN crack1, crack2, loc

// 3. Best encoder for conditions
MATCH (tr:TrainingRun)-[:USES_MODEL]->(m:Model),
      (tr)-[:TRAINED_ON]->(ds:Dataset)-[:CONTAINS_IMAGE]->(img:Image),
      (tr)-[:PRODUCED_CHECKPOINT]->(ckpt:Checkpoint)
WHERE img.exif_iso > 800  // Low-light
  AND ds.size < 500        // Small dataset
RETURN m.encoder, AVG(ckpt.val_iou) as avg_iou
ORDER BY avg_iou DESC

These queries are natural in Neo4j, impossible in ChromaDB.

docs.title: Decision Point: Issue #316 Evaluation
docs.text:
After 3 months of RAG production (ChromaDB), evaluate whether knowledge graphs (Neo4j) are justified.

Proceed with Neo4j IF: 1. ✅ Users frequently ask complex relationship questions 2. ✅ Data volume >= 50 projects and 200+ training runs 3. ✅ ChromaDB RAG limitations are significant 4. ✅ Budget allows ($135-320K Year 1) 5. ✅ Team has or can acquire Neo4j expertise

Consider Alternatives IF: 1. ⚠️ Query needs are simpler than expected 2. ⚠️ Data volume is small (<50 projects) 3. ⚠️ Budget is constrained 4. ⚠️ RAG enhancements can solve 80% of needs

Alternatives to Neo4j: - Streamlit Dashboard: SQL queries over JSON exports ($40-90K, 4-6 weeks) - NetworkX: Lightweight Python graph (<100K nodes, $60-150K, 6-10 weeks) - Enhanced RAG: Better metadata filtering in ChromaDB ($20-60K, 2-4 weeks)

docs.title: 1. Pinecone
docs.text:
Type: Managed vector database (SaaS)

Pros: - ✅ Fully managed, serverless - ✅ Excellent scalability (100M+ vectors) - ✅ Low latency (<10ms for billions of vectors) - ✅ Built-in features: hybrid search, namespaces, metadata filtering

Cons: - ❌ Closed-source, proprietary - ❌ Expensive ($70-1000+/month depending on usage) - ❌ Vendor lock-in (data export can be difficult) - ❌ Overkill for small projects (<1M vectors)

When to Choose Pinecone: - Enterprise with budget for managed service - Need to scale to 100M+ vectors - Want zero operational overhead - Global distribution requirements

For Crackz: Not recommended (overkill, expensive, vendor lock-in)

docs.title: 2. Weaviate
docs.text:
Type: Open-source vector database

Pros: - ✅ Open-source with enterprise support - ✅ Built-in vectorization (no need for external embedding model) - ✅ GraphQL API (in addition to REST) - ✅ Multi-modal (text, images, audio) - ✅ Hybrid search (vector + keyword + BM25)

Cons: - ❌ More complex setup than ChromaDB - ❌ Requires separate server (no embedded mode) - ❌ Heavier resource requirements - ❌ GraphQL learning curve

When to Choose Weaviate: - Need multi-tenancy - Want built-in vectorization - Building multi-modal search - Need production-grade features without vendor lock-in

For Crackz: Possible alternative if embedded mode isn't sufficient, but more complex than needed

docs.title: 3. Qdrant
docs.text:
Type: Open-source vector database (Rust-based)

Pros: - ✅ Rust-based (extremely fast) - ✅ Sophisticated filtering (better than ChromaDB) - ✅ Open-source with cloud offering - ✅ Payload storage (no external database needed for metadata) - ✅ Collections and partitioning

Cons: - ❌ Smaller ecosystem than ChromaDB/Pinecone - ❌ Less documentation for Python integration - ❌ No embedded mode (requires server)

When to Choose Qdrant: - Performance is critical (need fastest possible queries) - Complex metadata filtering requirements - Willing to run separate server

For Crackz: Good alternative if performance becomes bottleneck

docs.title: 4. FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search)
docs.text:
Type: Library (not a database)

Pros: - ✅ Extremely fast (GPU-accelerated) - ✅ Facebook-backed, mature - ✅ No server needed (pure library) - ✅ Highly optimized for ANN search

Cons: - ❌ No persistence layer (must implement yourself) - ❌ No metadata filtering - ❌ No HTTP API (Python/C++ only) - ❌ More complex to integrate

When to Choose FAISS: - Research projects or experiments - Maximum speed is required - Already have storage/persistence solution - Need GPU acceleration

For Crackz: Not recommended (no persistence, manual integration)

docs.title: 5. Elasticsearch (with vector support)
docs.text:
Type: Search engine with vector plugin

Pros: - ✅ Mature, widely used - ✅ Excellent full-text search - ✅ Can combine vector + keyword + filters in one query - ✅ Rich ecosystem and tooling

Cons: - ❌ Overkill (designed for full-text, not primarily vectors) - ❌ Complex setup (JVM, heap tuning) - ❌ Vector support is secondary feature - ❌ Higher resource requirements

When to Choose Elasticsearch: - Already using Elasticsearch - Need powerful full-text search + vectors - Have ops team familiar with ES

For Crackz: Not recommended (too complex, overkill)

Recommendation for Crackz RAG: Stick with ChromaDB - ✅ Embedded mode eliminates infrastructure overhead - ✅ Simple API reduces development time - ✅ Open-source avoids vendor lock-in - ✅ Sufficient for expected scale (50-100K vectors) - ✅ Good Python integration

docs.title: 1. ArangoDB
docs.text:
Type: Multi-model database (document + graph + key-value)

Pros: - ✅ Multi-model (flexible data storage) - ✅ AQL query language (easier than Cypher for some) - ✅ Open-source with managed cloud - ✅ Good performance

Cons: - ❌ Less mature graph algorithms than Neo4j - ❌ Smaller community - ❌ Graph features not as deep as Neo4j

When to Choose ArangoDB: - Need flexibility across data models - Don't want separate databases for docs + graphs - AQL is preferred over Cypher

For Crackz: Possible if multi-model flexibility is valuable

docs.title: 2. TigerGraph
docs.text:
Type: Native parallel graph database

Pros: - ✅ Fastest performance (12-8000x faster than competitors in benchmarks) - ✅ Native parallel processing - ✅ Real-time deep link analytics - ✅ GSQL query language

Cons: - ❌ Expensive (enterprise licensing) - ❌ Complex setup and tuning - ❌ Smaller ecosystem than Neo4j - ❌ GSQL learning curve

When to Choose TigerGraph: - Massive scale (trillions of relationships) - Real-time analytics are critical - Have large budget for licensing

For Crackz: Not recommended (overkill, expensive)

docs.title: 3. NetworkX (Python Library)
docs.text:
Type: Python graph library (in-memory)

Pros: - ✅ Pure Python (no server needed) - ✅ Excellent for graph analysis and algorithms - ✅ Free and open-source - ✅ Easy to learn and use - ✅ Great for prototyping

Cons: - ❌ In-memory only (no persistence without custom code) - ❌ Not designed for large graphs (>100K nodes gets slow) - ❌ No query language (Python code only) - ❌ Not suitable for production at scale

When to Choose NetworkX: - Small graphs (<100K nodes) - Prototyping and analysis - Don't want to manage a database server - Python-only project

For Crackz: Recommended as alternative to Neo4j if: - Data volume stays small (<100 projects) - Budget is very constrained - Want to defer infrastructure complexity

Example NetworkX Implementation: 

import networkx as nx

# Create in-memory graph
graph = nx.DiGraph()

# Add nodes and relationships
graph.add_node("ckpt_001", type="checkpoint", val_iou=0.87)
graph.add_node("model_001", type="model", encoder="resnet34")
graph.add_edge("ckpt_001", "model_001", relationship="USES_MODEL")

# Query
checkpoints = [n for n, d in graph.nodes(data=True)
               if d.get("type") == "checkpoint" and d.get("val_iou") > 0.85]

# Save to disk (JSON)
import json
data = nx.node_link_data(graph)
with open("graph.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f)

docs.title: 4. OrientDB
docs.text:
Type: Multi-model database (graph + document)

Pros: - ✅ Multi-model flexibility - ✅ SQL-like query language (familiar) - ✅ Open-source

Cons: - ❌ Less active development than Neo4j - ❌ Smaller community - ❌ Performance issues at large scale - ❌ Limited graph algorithm support

When to Choose OrientDB: - Budget-constrained - Want SQL-like queries - Need document + graph in one database

For Crackz: Not recommended (better alternatives exist)

docs.title: 5. Amazon Neptune
docs.text:
Type: Managed graph database (cloud)

Pros: - ✅ Fully managed (AWS) - ✅ Supports both property graph (Gremlin) and RDF (SPARQL) - ✅ High availability built-in - ✅ Integration with AWS ecosystem

Cons: - ❌ AWS vendor lock-in - ❌ Expensive ($0.10-0.80/hour = $70-600/month minimum) - ❌ Gremlin is less intuitive than Cypher - ❌ No desktop/local version for development

When to Choose Neptune: - Already heavily invested in AWS - Need managed service - Want RDF/SPARQL support

For Crackz: Not recommended (vendor lock-in, expensive)

Recommendation for Crackz Knowledge Graph:

If proceeding (Phase 2 evaluation says "Go"): - ✅ Neo4j Aura Professional ($65-500/month managed cloud) - Avoids operational overhead - Scales with usage - Enterprise-grade reliability

If deferring or simplifying: - ⚠️ NetworkX for prototype/small scale - Pure Python, no infrastructure - Easy to migrate to Neo4j later if needed - ⚠️ Streamlit Dashboard with SQL for analytics - Pre-aggregate data from JSON files - 80% of value at 20% of cost

docs.title: Can ChromaDB and Neo4j Work Together?
docs.text: YES! In fact, this is increasingly common in production systems. The combination provides: - ChromaDB: Semantic search over unstructured text - Neo4j: Relationship analysis over structured data - Together: Comprehensive knowledge system

docs.title: Simple Heuristics
docs.text:
class QueryRouter:
    def route_query(self, user_question: str) -> dict:
        """Determine which systems to query."""
        question_lower = user_question.lower()

        needs_vector = False
        needs_graph = False

        # Semantic search indicators
        if any(word in question_lower for word in ["how", "what", "explain", "guide", "documentation"]):
            needs_vector = True

        # Graph query indicators
        if any(word in question_lower for word in ["best", "optimal", "which", "compare", "relationship"]):
            needs_graph = True

        # Specific patterns
        if "works best for" in question_lower or "optimal" in question_lower:
            needs_graph = True

        if "does the documentation say" in question_lower:
            needs_vector = True

        return {
            "use_chromadb": needs_vector,
            "use_neo4j": needs_graph
        }

docs.title: LLM-Powered Routing
docs.text:
async def route_query_with_llm(self, user_question: str) -> dict:
    """Use LLM to determine query routing."""
    prompt = f"""
    Analyze this question and determine if it needs:
    1. Semantic search (ChromaDB): Find similar documents, explanations, guides
    2. Graph query (Neo4j): Analyze relationships, find optimal choices, compare entities

    Question: {user_question}

    Return JSON:
    {{
        "needs_semantic_search": true/false,
        "needs_graph_query": true/false,
        "reasoning": "brief explanation"
    }}
    """

    # Fast LLM call (Haiku for speed)
    response = await claude_client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )

    return json.loads(response.content[0].text)

docs.title: Workflow 1: Hybrid Query
docs.text:
User: "What are the best encoders for harbor crack detection, and what does the documentation say about training them?"

Routing: - ✅ ChromaDB: "what does the documentation say" → Semantic search - ✅ Neo4j: "best encoders for harbor" → Graph analytical query

Execution: 

async def execute_hybrid_query(query: str):
    # Parallel retrieval
    chroma_results, neo4j_results = await asyncio.gather(
        retrieve_from_chromadb(query),
        query_neo4j_graph(query)
    )

    # ChromaDB: Semantic search for training documentation
    chroma_context = """
    ## Documentation on Training Encoders
    [Retrieved from docs/training-guide.md]
    - ResNet family: Good all-around performance, start with resnet34
    - EfficientNet: Better for limited data (<500 images)
    - Training tips: Use transfer learning, pre-trained ImageNet weights
    """

    # Neo4j: Historical performance data
    neo4j_context = """
    ## Best Encoders for Harbor (Historical Data)
    Based on 45 training runs on harbor datasets:
    1. efficientnet-b2: Avg IoU 0.89 (12 runs)
    2. resnet50: Avg IoU 0.86 (18 runs)
    3. resnet34: Avg IoU 0.84 (15 runs)
    """

    # Aggregate contexts
    combined = f"{chroma_context}\n\n{neo4j_context}"

    # RAG with Claude
    answer = await claude.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
        system=f"Context:\n{combined}",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": query}]
    )

    return answer

Response:

"Based on historical performance data, EfficientNet-B2 performs best for harbor crack detection with an average IoU of 0.89 across 12 training runs.

According to the training documentation, EfficientNet is particularly well-suited for limited data scenarios (<500 images), which is often the case in harbor infrastructure projects.

Recommendation: Start with encoder: efficientnet-b2 in your project YAML. Use transfer learning with pre-trained ImageNet weights for best results."

docs.title: Implementation for Crackz
docs.text:
# From Issue #314 (RAG Integration) with KG extension
class AIChatServiceWithKG(AIChatService):
    """Enhanced AI chat with both RAG and Knowledge Graph."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        async_loop: AsyncEventLoop,
        app_state: AppState,
        api_key: str,
        model: str = "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
        enable_rag: bool = True,
        enable_kg: bool = False,  # Conditional on Phase 3
        rag_index_path: Path | None = None,
        kg_api: KnowledgeGraphAPI | None = None
    ):
        super().__init__(async_loop, app_state, api_key, model)

        self.enable_rag = enable_rag
        self.enable_kg = enable_kg

        # Initialize retrieval systems
        if enable_rag and rag_index_path:
            self.rag_retriever = RAGRetriever(rag_index_path)
        else:
            self.rag_retriever = None

        if enable_kg and kg_api:
            self.kg_api = kg_api
        else:
            self.kg_api = None

    async def _call_claude_api(self) -> str:
        """Enhanced RAG with optional KG integration."""
        client = self._get_client()

        # Base system prompt
        system_prompt = self._build_base_system_prompt()

        # Existing project context
        project_context = self._get_context()

        # Get last user message
        last_message = self.conversation_history[-1].content if self.conversation_history else ""

        # Initialize contexts
        rag_context = ""
        kg_context = ""

        # Route query (determine what to query)
        routing = await self._route_query(last_message)

        # Retrieve from ChromaDB if needed
        if self.rag_retriever and routing["use_rag"]:
            rag_docs = await self.rag_retriever.retrieve(
                query=last_message,
                k=5,
                filters={"project": self.app_state.project.name} if self.app_state.project else {}
            )
            rag_context = self._format_rag_context(rag_docs)

        # Query Neo4j if needed
        if self.kg_api and routing["use_kg"]:
            kg_results = await self._execute_kg_queries(last_message, routing)
            kg_context = self._format_kg_context(kg_results)

        # Combine all contexts
        full_system_prompt = f"""
        {system_prompt}

        {project_context}

        ## Retrieved Documentation (RAG)
        {rag_context}

        ## Analytical Data (Knowledge Graph)
        {kg_context}

        Use the retrieved information to provide accurate, specific answers.
        Cite sources from documentation and reference data from historical analysis.
        """

        # Call Claude with enhanced context
        response = await client.messages.create(
            model=self.model,
            max_tokens=2048,
            system=full_system_prompt,
            messages=[{"role": msg.role, "content": msg.content}
                     for msg in self.conversation_history]
        )

        return response.content[0].text

    async def _route_query(self, query: str) -> dict:
        """Determine which systems to query."""
        # Simple heuristic routing
        query_lower = query.lower()

        return {
            "use_rag": any(word in query_lower for word in ["how", "what", "documentation", "guide", "explain"]),
            "use_kg": any(word in query_lower for word in ["best", "optimal", "which", "compare", "performance"])
        }

    async def _execute_kg_queries(self, query: str, routing: dict) -> dict:
        """Execute appropriate knowledge graph queries."""
        results = {}

        # Pattern matching for specific query types
        if "best encoder" in query.lower():
            results["encoder_performance"] = self.kg_api.find_best_encoder_for_conditions()

        if "crack progression" in query.lower() or "worsened" in query.lower():
            # Extract GPS from query (simplified)
            results["crack_progression"] = self.kg_api.track_crack_progression()

        if "hyperparameter" in query.lower() or "optimal parameters" in query.lower():
            results["hyperparameters"] = self.kg_api.get_optimal_hyperparameters()

        return results

docs.title: Overhead and Complexity
docs.text:
Pros of Hybrid: - ✅ Comprehensive answers (semantic + analytical) - ✅ Best tool for each job - ✅ Higher quality responses - ✅ More flexible query handling

Cons of Hybrid: - ❌ 2x infrastructure (ChromaDB + Neo4j) - ❌ 2x query latency (even with parallelization) - ❌ More complex code (routing logic, aggregation) - ❌ Higher development cost (+2-3 weeks) - ❌ More operational overhead (2 systems to monitor)

Cost Impact: - Development: +$20-45K (query router, aggregation, testing) - Infrastructure: +$65-500/month (Neo4j Aura) - Maintenance: +4-8 hours/month (monitoring both systems)

Total Hybrid Cost (Year 1): - ChromaDB alone: $45-125K - Neo4j alone: $135-320K - Hybrid (both): $180-445K

When Hybrid Makes Sense: - High query diversity (both semantic and analytical queries are frequent) - Budget allows for dual infrastructure - User needs justify the complexity - Team can support both systems

Recommendation for Crackz: - Phase 1: Start with ChromaDB only - Phase 2: Evaluate after 3 months - Phase 3: Add Neo4j only if validated (hybrid usage becomes automatic)

docs.title: When to Use ChromaDB
docs.text:
✅ Always use ChromaDB if you need: - Semantic search over unstructured text - RAG for LLM applications - Finding similar documents/items by content - Quick prototyping with minimal infrastructure - Embedded database (no separate server)

✅ ChromaDB is the right choice when: - Data is primarily textual (docs, logs, summaries) - Queries are about similarity ("find related") - Relationships are implicit or simple - Budget is constrained - Need fast time-to-value

❌ Don't use ChromaDB for: - Complex relationship queries - Graph traversal (lineage, multi-hop) - Transactional updates across entities - Analytical aggregations across relationships

docs.title: When to Use Neo4j
docs.text:
✅ Always use Neo4j if you need: - Complex relationship analysis - Graph traversal (multi-hop queries) - Lineage tracking (parent-child chains) - Pattern detection in networks - Graph algorithms (centrality, community detection)

✅ Neo4j is the right choice when: - Data is highly interconnected - Relationships are first-class (as important as entities) - Queries involve "how are they connected?" - Need transactional consistency - Analytical queries across relationship paths

❌ Don't use Neo4j for: - Simple similarity search - Vector embeddings (use vector database) - Full-text search (use Elasticsearch) - Time-series metrics (use InfluxDB)

docs.title: When to Use Both (Hybrid)
docs.text:
✅ Use both ChromaDB + Neo4j when: - Need comprehensive knowledge system - Both semantic search AND relationship queries are frequent - Budget allows dual infrastructure - Query diversity justifies complexity - Users ask hybrid questions ("What's the best X, and what do docs say about it?")

⚠️ Consider hybrid carefully because: - 2x infrastructure complexity - Higher development and operational costs - Query routing logic required - May be overkill if one system covers 80% of needs

docs.title: Decision Tree for Crackz
docs.text:
START
  ↓
Q1: Do you need semantic search over documentation?
  YES → Use ChromaDB (Phase 1 RAG)
  NO → Skip RAG (unlikely for Crackz)
  ↓
Q2: After 3 months RAG, do users frequently ask relationship queries?
  YES → Continue to Q3
  NO → Stick with ChromaDB only, enhance with better metadata filtering
  ↓
Q3: Do you have 50+ projects and 200+ training runs?
  YES → Continue to Q4
  NO → Consider NetworkX lightweight graph OR defer until data grows
  ↓
Q4: Can you allocate $135-320K for knowledge graph?
  YES → Proceed with Neo4j (Phase 3)
  NO → Build Streamlit dashboard OR NetworkX lightweight graph
  ↓
END: Use ChromaDB + [Neo4j OR NetworkX OR Streamlit Dashboard]

docs.title: Q: Can I start with ChromaDB and add Neo4j later?
docs.text: A: Yes! This is the recommended approach (see Phase 1 → Phase 2 → Phase 3). Start with RAG, validate need, then add knowledge graph.

docs.title: Q: Will ChromaDB handle 1M+ vectors?
docs.text: A: Yes, but you'll need to use client-server mode or cloud mode instead of embedded mode. For Crackz's estimated 50-100K vectors, embedded mode is sufficient.

docs.title: Q: Can I use ChromaDB for relationship queries?
docs.text: A: No, not natively. You can use metadata filtering for simple relationships, but complex multi-hop queries require a graph database.

docs.title: Q: Is Neo4j free?
docs.text: A: The Community Edition is free (open-source), but lacks clustering and some enterprise features. Desktop is free for development. Aura (cloud) has a free tier with limitations. Enterprise Edition requires licensing.

docs.title: Q: How do I migrate from ChromaDB to another vector database?
docs.text: A: ChromaDB supports export to standard formats. Most vector databases have import tools. Migration is relatively straightforward (export embeddings, re-import).

docs.title: Q: How do I migrate from NetworkX to Neo4j?
docs.text: A: NetworkX can export to JSON or GraphML formats. Neo4j can import these via LOAD CSV or APOC procedures. Design your NetworkX schema with future Neo4j migration in mind.

docs.title: Q: What's the minimum hardware for Neo4j?
docs.text: A: 4GB RAM, 2 CPU cores, 10GB storage for small deployments. Recommended: 16GB RAM, 4 cores, 50GB+ storage for production.

docs.title: Q: Can I run Neo4j and ChromaDB on the same machine?
docs.text: A: Yes! They use different ports and resources. A machine with 16GB RAM can comfortably run both for small-medium workloads.

docs.title: Q: What happens if my query needs both semantic search AND graph traversal?
docs.text: A: Use the hybrid architecture described in this document. Query both systems in parallel, aggregate results, then use an LLM to generate a comprehensive answer.

docs.title: Q: How much does it cost to embed 100K documents?
docs.text:
A: With OpenAI text-embedding-3-small: 100K docs × avg 200 tokens = 20M tokens × $0.00002/1K = $0.40. Very cheap. You can also use free local models like Sentence Transformers.

docs.title: Report Generation
docs.text: Generate professional Word documents with detection results and analysis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The reporting feature creates branded Microsoft Word documents (.docx) containing:

  • Project Information: Name, description, creation date
  • Detection Statistics: Total images analyzed, detection rate, average confidence
  • Severity Breakdown: Distribution of crack severity levels
  • Sample Images: Representative detection results organized by severity
  • Anaxiatech Branding: Company logo, colors, and contact information

Reports are ideal for sharing inspection results with clients, stakeholders, or archival purposes.

docs.title: Basic Report Generation
docs.text:
Generate a report for your project:

crackz report generate --project demo-project

This creates demo-project_report.docx in the project directory.

docs.title: Custom Output Path
docs.text:
Specify where to save the report:

crackz report generate --project demo-project --output inspection_report.docx

docs.title: Using Config File
docs.text:
Generate from a YAML configuration:

crackz report generate --cfg project_config.yaml --output report.docx

docs.title: 1. Header Section
docs.text:
• Anaxiatech logo (automatically included if available)
  • Document title: "Harbor Infrastructure Inspection Report"
  • Subtitle: "Crack Detection Analysis"
  • Generation date: Timestamp when report was created

docs.title: 2. Project Information
docs.text: A table containing: - Project name - Description - Creation date

docs.title: 3. Detection Statistics
docs.text: Summary metrics including: - Total images analyzed - Number of images with detected cracks - Overall detection rate (%) - Average confidence level (%)

docs.title: 4. Severity Breakdown
docs.text:
Distribution of results by confidence level: - Crack Detected: High confidence detections (≥5% default) - Probable Crack: Medium confidence (2-5% default) - Possible Crack: Low confidence (0.5-2% default) - No Crack: Below detection threshold

Each severity level shows: - Number of images - Percentage of total - Color-coded for easy identification

docs.title: 5. Detection Results
docs.text:
Sample images organized by severity (up to 5 images per category): - Original filename - Detection visualization images with crack overlays and heatmaps - Confidence percentage - Crack area percentage (when available)

The report includes the actual detection visualization images showing: - Red/yellow overlay highlighting detected cracks - Color-coded intensity based on detection confidence - Visual representation of the AI's crack detection

Note: Images are automatically resized to fit page width while maintaining aspect ratio. Large image sets show a representative sample with a note about complete results.

docs.title: 6. Company Information
docs.text:
• About Anaxiatech section
  • Contact information (email, website)
  • Disclaimer about AI-generated results

docs.title: Severity Thresholds
docs.text:
Confidence thresholds are configured in your project's detection settings:

ai:
  detection:
    min_confidence: 0.005      # 0.5% - Possible Crack threshold
    medium_confidence: 0.02    # 2% - Probable Crack threshold
    high_confidence: 0.05      # 5% - Crack Detected threshold

Adjust these values to control how detections are categorized in reports.

docs.title: Image Limits
docs.text:
By default, reports include up to 5 sample images per severity level to keep file sizes manageable. This prevents extremely large documents when processing hundreds or thousands of images.

For complete results, refer to the project's detections/ directory.
